title: British & German East Africa
titleline: British & German East Africa - The History Web
para1: British and German East Africa were colonial territories carved from the region in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. Germany took Tanganyika, Rwanda, and Burundi, claims staked from 1884 by agents of the German East Africa Company and recognized by the European powers, while Britain held Kenya and Uganda, its gateway to the headwaters of the Nile. Together they matter because their borders became those of modern Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Kenya, and Uganda.
para2: Both powers ruled through forced labor and cash crops: Germany pushed cotton and sisal, and when its exactions provoked the Maji Maji rebellion of 1905, it crushed the rising with a famine that killed hundreds of thousands. Britain built the Uganda Railway from Mombasa to Lake Victoria, the Lunatic Line, settled whites on Kenya's highlands, and leaned on African allies like the kingdom of Buganda. On the coast the colonizers inherited a far older world: Swahili ports such as Mombasa had admitted the goods of Arabian and Asian traders into the continent for many centuries. Inland, the cool highlands around the Rift Valley became the focus of European settlement, their tea plantations an economic staple of the colonial era.
para3: The First World War ended German rule: after a remarkable guerrilla campaign by the German commander Lettow Vorbeck, the colony fell to Allied forces, and the Treaty of Versailles handed most of it to Britain as the Tanganyika mandate, with Rwanda and Burundi going to Belgium.
para4: Independence movements transformed the map in the early 1960s: Tanganyika united with Zanzibar to form Tanzania, while Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda, and Burundi all won sovereignty, each still living with borders, economies, and tensions drafted in the colonial decades.

title: French North Africa
titleline: French North Africa - The History Web
para1: French North Africa refers to Algeria, Tunisia, and Morocco under French colonial rule. France invaded Algeria in 1830, chasing pirates and glory, and stayed 132 years; it added protectorates over Tunisia in 1881 and Morocco in 1912, until the whole western Maghreb flew the tricolor. The region matters because nowhere else in Africa did settler colonialism dig so deep, or end so bloodily.
para2: Algeria was the jewel and the wound: conquered in decades of brutal campaigning, it was legally made part of France itself, its lands handed to a settler minority, the colons or pieds noirs, who numbered a tenth of the population and ruled the rest through laws that made Muslims second class in their own country. Land confiscation, language loss, and periodic famine marked Algerian life under France. The pattern was set early: once resistance was crushed, cultivable land was confiscated wholesale, and laws such as the sénatus-consulte of 1863 broke up tribal holdings, driving Algerian peasants onto marginal lands. Paris itself was ambivalent: Napoleon III declared Algeria not a French province but an Arab country, a European colony, and a French camp, yet after his fall in 1870 the settlers took what they wanted, crushing the great Kabylia uprising of 1871 and parcelling out the land.
para3: Tunisia and Morocco fared somewhat differently as protectorates, their sultans and bey left nominally reigning while French residents general ruled, but land and power flowed the same way. In Morocco the French cultivated the Alaouite monarchy as partner, a choice that eased their eventual exit.
para4: Decolonization split along the same lines: Tunisia and Morocco won independence peacefully in 1956, but Algeria, home to a million settlers, exploded into a war of independence from 1954 to 1962 of legendary savagery, ending with the flight of the pieds noirs and a free Algeria. French rule left lasting economic and cultural marks, the French language above all, and a relationship of intimacy and resentment that endures on both shores of the Mediterranean.

title: Italian Colonization of the Horn of Africa
titleline: Italian Colonization of the Horn of Africa - The History Web
para1: Italian Colonization of the Horn of Africa began with Eritrea, which Italy pieced together from Red Sea ports and highlands in the late 19th century, naming it its first colony in 1890. Asmara, once a mere highland hamlet, became the colonial capital in 1900, rebuilt as a planned modern city on the plateau and served by the Eritrean Railway. Flush with imperial ambition, Italy then invaded Ethiopia in 1895, only to suffer at Adwa in 1896 the most famous defeat a European power ever suffered in Africa, leaving Ethiopia proudly independent and Italy deeply humiliated.
para2: Italy also took Italian Somaliland along the Horn's eastern coast, and in 1911 to 1912 it seized Libya from the Ottomans. Its rule in the Horn was authoritarian and racially stratified, and its ambitions never rested: fascist Italy under Mussolini vowed to avenge Adwa.
para3: The revenge came with poison gas and aircraft: in 1935 to 1936 Italy invaded Ethiopia again, this time conquering it despite heroic resistance, and proclaimed its short lived Italian East Africa empire. Emperor Haile Selassie carried his nation's cause to the League of Nations, which did nothing, a failure that foreshadowed the world war to come.
para4: Italian rule over Ethiopia lasted barely five years: in 1941 British and Commonwealth forces, fighting alongside Ethiopian patriots, liberated the Horn, and after the war Italy lost its colonies for good. Eritrea was soon federated with Ethiopia, Federation curdled into annexation, and Eritreans fought a bitter war of independence lasting nearly three decades before winning sovereignty in 1993. Somalia became independent in 1960, and the legacies of that violent decade, borders, resentments, and memories of resistance, still shape the Horn today.

title: Muhammad Ali's Egypt
titleline: Muhammad Ali's Egypt - The History Web
para1: Muhammad Ali's Egypt refers to the state created by the Ottoman Albanian military commander who seized power in Egypt following the retreat of Napoleon's French forces, ruling as the sultan's viceroy from 1805 to 1848. Born in Kavala in Macedonia, he arrived in Egypt in 1801 with an Albanian regiment sent to expel the French, and by sheer political skill had himself named governor within four years. He is widely regarded as the founder of modern Egypt.
para2: Muhammad Ali eliminated the ancient Mamluk political class, most brutally in 1811, when he invited their leaders to a celebration at the Cairo citadel and had them cut down. Then he rebuilt the state from the ground up: by 1815 most farmland had become state land, irrigation was renewed, new cash crops like cotton spread across the Delta, and factories, docks, and a modern army of conscripted Egyptian peasants, officered by Turks and trained by Europeans, rose on the proceeds.
para3: His ambitions reached far beyond Egypt: his armies campaigned in Arabia, conquered the Sudan in search of gold and recruits, and nearly toppled the sultan himself, winning Syria after 1831 and crushing the Ottoman army at Nizip in 1839. Only the European powers stopped him: they destroyed his fleet at Navarino in 1827 and forced him out of Syria in 1840, settling him instead with the hereditary rule of Egypt and Sudan.
para4: This period matters because it rapidly transformed an impoverished Ottoman province into a self-sustaining regional power with a modern conscript military, Western style schools, and Europe's closest thing to an industrial economy outside Europe itself. Though many reforms faded after his death in 1849, his dynasty ruled Egypt until 1952, and he had cleared the path for an independent Egyptian state.

title: Ottoman North Africa
titleline: Ottoman North Africa - The History Web
para1: Ottoman North Africa refers to the autonomous regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli established along the Maghreb coastline following the 16th century conquests. The Ottomans arrived almost by invitation: Algiers accepted Sultan Selim's suzerainty in 1517 under the corsair brothers Aruj and Hayreddin Barbarossa, and Tunis entered Ottoman rule under Suleiman the Magnificent in 1534, leaving Morocco, which fought the Ottomans off, as the one Maghreb state outside the empire.
para2: Governed by local military elites, janissaries, and corsair captains, these coastal enclaves operated with near total independence from the distant sultan in Istanbul, who was content with tribute and naval support. The arrangement made the empire a Mediterranean superpower: Hayreddin Barbarossa, commanding the Ottoman fleet, smashed a Christian alliance at Preveza in 1538 and ruled the western sea for a generation.
para3: This era matters because it turned the Barbary Coast into a naval force that shaped Western Mediterranean trade and grew rich on state sponsored privateering and maritime tolls, while the regency cities, Algiers above all, blossomed with mosques, palaces, and one of the most cosmopolitan ports of the age. Over time each regency settled into its own ruling order: elected deys in Algiers, and hereditary dynasties in Tunis and Tripoli. The wider empire's sea power framed everything: the Ottoman navy, built to titanic scale under Suleiman, dominated the Mediterranean until its defeat at Lepanto in 1571, and its slow waning from the 17th century left the regencies increasingly on their own.
para4: Reliance on corsair raids, however, repeatedly triggered naval blockades and military intervention by European nations and the young United States, while internal corruption, economic isolation, and declining naval supremacy eroded stability through the late 18th century. The era of Ottoman control ended abruptly in the 19th century: France invaded Algiers in 1830, beginning a wave of European colonial expansion that would swallow all of North Africa.

title: The Alaouite Dynasty
titleline: The Alaouite Dynasty - The History Web
para1: The Alaouite Dynasty is the ruling royal family of Morocco, coming to power in 1666 and remaining on the throne to the present day, one of the oldest reigning dynasties in the world. Originating from the oasis region of Tafilalt in the desert southeast, they claimed direct descent from the Prophet Muhammad, and used this sharifian legitimacy to unify a nation fractured by half a century of Saadi civil wars.
para2: This dynasty matters because it preserved Moroccan independence for centuries, repelling Ottoman expansion from the east and European encroachment along the coasts. Under the long, iron fisted rule of Sultan Moulay Ismail, who reigned from 1672 to 1727, Morocco built a formidable standing army, the Black Guard, and drove European garrisons out of key coastal strongholds like Tangier. Ismail raised a new imperial capital at Meknes, wrapping it in walls and monumental gates that still stand as a World Heritage city.
para3: The state developed sophisticated diplomacy: Morocco was among the very first nations to deal officially with the young United States, opening its ports to American ships in 1777 and signing a treaty of friendship in 1786 that remains America's longest unbroken treaty relationship. The dynasty weathered pirates, pretenders, and the long 19th century squeeze of European economic pressure.
para4: The hardest test came in 1912, when military defeats forced the sultan to accept a Franco Spanish protectorate, yet the dynasty kept its throne and its hold on Moroccan loyalty. When Sultan Mohammed V was exiled for backing the independence movement, his return in triumph made him the father of the nation: Morocco won full independence in 1956, and his grandson, King Mohammed VI, wears the Alaouite crown today.

title: The Ashanti Empire
titleline: The Ashanti Empire - The History Web
para1: The Ashanti Empire was a formidable Akan state that dominated the central goldfields and coastal forests of modern day Ghana from 1701 to 1901. It rose when Osei Tutu, king of Kumasi, united the small Asante chiefdoms to throw off their overlords, the Denkyera, whom his armies crushed around 1698 to 1701. It matters because it built one of the most sophisticated states of precolonial Africa, with a merit based bureaucracy, a road and message network, and an army that defied the British Empire for most of a century.
para2: The empire's soul was the Golden Stool: according to tradition, the priest Okomfo Anokye called it down from heaven onto Osei Tutu's knees, and it became the symbol of the Asante nation's unity, holier than any king, for kings were enthroned upon it but never sat in it. Every chief swore allegiance to it, and when the British later demanded to sit on it as governor, the Asante went to war.
para3: Wealth and war fed each other: Ashanti gold financed the state, while the slave trade with British and Dutch forts on the coast brought the firearms that drove expansion, until the empire stretched from the Comoe River to the Togo Mountains. Under Opoku Ware and the great kings who followed, government reached every village through territorial divisions, paramount chiefs, and queen mothers who advised and nominated.
para4: The end came slowly and then at once: after decades of friction over the coastal forts, a British expedition under Sir Garnet Wolseley marched on Kumasi in 1874 and held it for a day, a shock that broke the empire's confidence and sparked secessionist revolts. Resistance flared again in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, but on January 1, 1902, Asante was declared a British crown colony, though the Asantehene's stool, and his people, endured.

title: The Barbary States
titleline: The Barbary States - The History Web
para1: The Barbary States were the North African regencies of Algiers, Tunis, and Tripoli, ruled under loose Ottoman suzerainty from the 16th to the early 19th century. The very name Barbary, from the Berbers of the coast, became a byword in Europe for piracy, and these states matter because for three centuries their corsairs made every power on the Mediterranean pay attention, and pay up.
para2: The corsairs were the engine of the system: swift galleys out of Algiers and Tunis raided shipping and coasts from Spain to Iceland, seizing cargoes and captives who were ransomed, sold, or put to the oars. The Ottomans had a genius for recruiting their enemies: many of the most feared corsair captains were European renegades, men like Yusuf Rais, born Jack Birdy in England, who turned their skills to the Barbary flag. European states found it cheaper to pay annual tribute for safe passage than to fight, and even the new United States, fresh from revolution, paid protection money until President Jefferson sent warships instead.
para3: Fighting came in waves: American squadrons battled Tripoli from 1801 and returned under Decatur in 1815 to force an end to tribute, while a British fleet under Lord Exmouth bombarded Algiers in 1816 to free Christian captives. Each blow weakened the corsair economy, and the rulers, deys in Algiers, beys in Tunis, pashas and local dynasties in Tripoli, could no longer command the sea that fed them.
para4: The end came from France: in 1830 a French army landed and took Algiers, beginning a conquest of Algeria that would last generations and opening the door to the European colonization of North Africa. The Barbary system collapsed with it, and the old corsair ports became colonial cities.

title: The Boer Republics
titleline: The Boer Republics - The History Web
para1: The Boer Republics were independent, self governing nations established in the interior of Southern Africa by Dutch descended settlers, the Boers, who quit British ruled Cape Colony in the Great Trek of the 1830s. Some fourteen thousand trekkers moved north with their wagons, fighting the Ndebele and the Zulu for land, and by the mid 1850s they had founded the two republics that mattered most: the South African Republic, the Transvaal, and the Orange Free State.
para2: The trek was soaked in blood and legend: the Zulu king Dingane massacred the trek leader Piet Retief and his party after inviting them to his kraal, and at the Battle of Blood River in 1838 Andries Pretorius and his riflemen broke a Zulu army, a victory that became the founding myth of Afrikaner nationhood. The republics that followed were conservative, God fearing farming states, governed by white male voters under constitutions mixing Boer custom with Dutch and American ideas.
para3: The republics might have remained obscure pastoral backwaters but for geology: diamonds at Kimberley in the late 1860s and, above all, the world's richest gold reef on the Witwatersrand in 1886 transformed the Transvaal overnight, flooding it with foreign fortune seekers the Boers refused to enfranchise. Gold made the republics worth having, and Britain moved to take them.
para4: The result was the South African War of 1899 to 1902, a grinding struggle of commandos against empire that ended with the republics annexed as British colonies. In 1910 they joined the Cape and Natal in the Union of South Africa, and the defeated Boers, now Afrikaners, set about winning through politics what they had lost in war, with consequences that shaped South Africa for the rest of the century.

title: The Buganda Kingdom
titleline: The Buganda Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Buganda Kingdom was a powerful, highly centralized state on the northern shores of Lake Victoria in modern day Uganda. Founded in the late 14th century among the Bantu speaking Ganda people, it expanded rapidly from the 18th through the 19th century until it stood as the largest and most powerful kingdom in the entire region. It matters because its disciplined government made it the model African state in European eyes, and because its fierce sense of identity has shaped Uganda's politics ever since.
para2: At its head ruled an absolute monarch, the kabaka, who governed through an efficient bureaucracy: the chiefs of conquered lands ruled as his personal appointees, not hereditary lords, so loyalty flowed straight to the throne. Buganda built a formidable navy of war canoes that commanded Lake Victoria, a network of broad, well kept roads, and a sizable standing army.
para3: The 19th century brought new faiths and new pressures: under Kabaka Mutesa I, Muslim traders and then Christian missionaries arrived at the kabaka's court, competing for converts, and after his death in 1884 the kingdom split into politico religious factions. Britain declared a sphere of influence in 1894, and the Buganda Agreement of 1900 made the kingdom a protectorate, one whose Ganda officials became pillars of the British administration across East Africa.
para4: Buganda's separate identity outlasted empire: at Uganda's independence in 1962 the kingdom won special federal status, but tensions with the central government exploded in 1966, when Prime Minister Milton Obote attacked the kabaka's palace and then abolished the kingdoms altogether. Buganda was restored in 1993, and the kabaka still reigns today, a king without a state but never without a people.

title: The Cape Colony
titleline: The Cape Colony - The History Web
para1: The Cape Colony was founded by the Dutch East India Company in 1652, when Jan van Riebeeck planted a refreshment station at Cape Town to feed the company's ships rounding Africa to Asia. From that garden grew a settler society: Dutch, French, and German colonists, the ancestors of the Afrikaners, along with enslaved people brought from Asia and Africa, and the Khoikhoi and San peoples whose lands were steadily swallowed.
para2: Britain seized the Cape in 1806, during the Napoleonic wars, and held it for over a century, expanding the colony's borders through wars and treaties against the Xhosa kingdoms on its eastern frontier. British rule brought English law and settlers, the abolition of slavery in the 1830s, which helped provoke the Boer Great Trek into the interior, the founding epic of Afrikaner nationhood: between 1835 and the early 1840s some 12,000 to 14,000 Boers, whole parties of kinfolk and neighbors, crossed the Orange River with their wagons and fought their way past the kingdoms of the interior with horses, guns, and laagered camps, and eventually diamonds and gold, which made the Cape the richest corner of Africa.
para3: The colony matters because so much of South Africa's later history was drafted there: a society built on land dispossession and racial hierarchy, a booming mining economy run on cheap African labor, and a qualified franchise that let some Black men vote, a flicker of inclusion snuffed out after union.
para4: In 1910 the Cape Colony joined Natal, the Transvaal, and the Orange Free State to form the Union of South Africa, becoming the Cape Province. Its racial laws and labor systems helped shape the apartheid that followed, and its story, from van Riebeeck's garden to Mandela's walk to freedom in Cape Town, remains the key to understanding South Africa.

title: The Ethiopian Empire (Menelik II)
titleline: The Ethiopian Empire (Menelik II) - The History Web
para1: The Ethiopian Empire under Emperor Menelik II was a rapidly modernizing Christian state that preserved its ancient sovereignty at the height of European imperialism in the late 19th century. King of Shewa before he was emperor, Menelik took the throne in 1889 and consolidated control over the regional warlords, then vastly expanded Ethiopia's southern and eastern borders to roughly their modern shape. He matters because under him Ethiopia did what almost no other African state managed: it beat a European power in open battle and stayed free.
para2: The crisis came from Italy, which had seized Eritrea and coveted the rest. The 1889 Treaty of Wuchale became famous for its trick: the Italian text made Ethiopia an Italian protectorate, while the Amharic text said no such thing, and when Menelik discovered the difference he denounced the treaty and prepared for war. His empress, Taitu, matched him in resolve; it was she who named his new capital Addis Ababa, the New Flower.
para3: On March 1, 1896, at the mountain village of Adwa, Menelik's army of a hundred thousand, supplied with modern rifles and united as Ethiopia had rarely been, destroyed the invading Italian colonial army in a single day. Adwa became a beacon: the victory of an African state over a European empire, celebrated ever after across the colonized world and deep in the Pan African imagination.
para4: Menelik used the peace to modernize: a railway from Djibouti toward the capital, telephone lines, a modern school and hospital, a national bank and currency. He reigned until 1913, leaving an empire doubled in size and unbowed, the one African kingdom whose flag never came down in the age of conquest.

title: The Ethiopian Empire (Tewodros II onward)
titleline: The Ethiopian Empire (Tewodros II onward) - The History Web
para1: This period covers Ethiopia's modern empire from Emperor Tewodros II in the mid 19th century, when the land was reunified after decades of princely division known as the Era of the Princes. Tewodros, a warrior of humble birth who fought his way to the throne in 1855, has been called Ethiopia's first modern ruler: he broke the great provinces into districts under his own appointees, tried to subordinate the church to the crown, and dreamed of a merit based army armed with modern cannon. Contemporary Europeans called him an Ethiopian Peter the Great, for his temper and his genius alike: he set the foreign missionaries at his court to casting his first cannon and imported English artisans to build an arms industry.
para2: His reach exceeded his grasp: the nobles rebelled, his modernization program stalled, and an unanswered letter to Queen Victoria festered into a diplomatic crisis. When Tewodros imprisoned British envoys and missionaries, Britain sent the Napier expedition, which defeated him at his mountain fortress of Magdala in April 1868; the emperor took his own life rather than surrender.
para3: His successors finished what he began: Yohannes IV defended the empire against Egyptians, Mahdists, and Italians, dying in battle against the Mahdists in 1889, and Menelik II expanded the empire to its modern borders, then defeated Italy at the battle of Adwa in 1896, a victory that preserved Ethiopian independence when almost all of Africa fell under colonial rule.
para4: The last emperor, Haile Selassie, ruled from 1930 to 1974, surviving Italian invasion and occupation in the 1930s and returning to modernize the state and make Ethiopia a voice of African dignity on the world stage. His overthrow by a military committee in 1974 ended the ancient monarchy, and the empire became a republic under revolutionary rule.

title: The Kingdom of Dahomey
titleline: The Kingdom of Dahomey - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Dahomey was a highly militarized Fon state in what is now the Republic of Benin, flourishing from about 1600 until 1894, with its palace capital at Abomey. Born a small dependency of the coastal kingdom of Allada, it seized its independence in the 17th century under King Wegbaja and then, under King Agaja in the early 18th century, conquered Allada and the great slave port of Ouidah, commanding the coast Europeans called the Slave Coast.
para2: Dahomey matters deeply to world history for its absolute, centralized monarchy and its most famous institution: the elite corps of women soldiers Europeans nicknamed the Dahomey Amazons, the Mino, who guarded the king, led his armies, and were feared across the region. The kings ran the state with remarkable discipline, counting their people and palm trees in regular censuses and monopolizing foreign trade.
para3: For two centuries the kingdom's economy turned on war and the slave trade: Dahomey's armies raided deep into the interior, and its kings sold captives at Ouidah in exchange for guns and goods, even as they paid grudging tribute to the Oyo Empire until shaking it off in the early 19th century. Under King Ghezo, who reigned from 1818, the kingdom pivoted toward palm oil as the Atlantic slave trade waned, and its wealth showed in the bas relief adorned palaces of Abomey.
para4: The end came from France: after disputes over the coast, French columns fought their way inland and captured Abomey in 1894, exiling the last independent king, Behanzin. Dahomey became a French colony, but its memory lives on in Benin, in the restored palaces of Abomey, and in the global fame of its women warriors.

title: The Kingdom of Ndongo and Matamba
titleline: The Kingdom of Ndongo and Matamba - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Ndongo and Matamba was a powerful West Central African state in modern day Angola, formed through the unification of two Mbundu kingdoms in the 17th century. The realm reached its height under the legendary Queen Nzinga, who took the throne and waged decades of strategic warfare and diplomacy against the Portuguese. This state matters because Nzinga's resistance made her one of the great figures of African history, a ruler who held a European empire at bay for nearly forty years.
para2: Nzinga first faced the Portuguese in 1622, negotiating a peace treaty on behalf of her brother the king: when the Portuguese offered her no chair, the story goes, she had a servant kneel as her seat, and negotiated as an equal. After her brother's death she seized power herself, converted to Catholicism as Ana de Souza when it served her, and broke with the Portuguese when it did not.
para3: Her statecraft was as flexible as her armies: she allied with the fierce Imbangala warriors, conquered the kingdom of Matamba to make it her base, and joined the Dutch in their war against Portugal in Angola, nearly driving the Europeans into the sea in the 1640s. Even when the Dutch withdrew, she fought on, raiding the slave trade that fed on her region and sheltering runaways in her lands.
para4: In old age Nzinga made peace on her own terms, securing recognition of her rule before her death in 1663, and her united realm of Ndongo and Matamba held off full Portuguese conquest for generations after her. Today she is Angola's greatest national heroine, a symbol of resistance taught across Africa and the diaspora.

title: The Mahdist State
titleline: The Mahdist State - The History Web
para1: The Mahdist State was an Islamic state established in Sudan between 1885 and 1899 following a massive uprising led by Muhammad Ahmad, a religious teacher who in 1881 proclaimed himself the Mahdi, the awaited deliverer of Islam. Mobilizing Sudanese tribes against oppressive Turco Egyptian rule and growing European interference, his followers, the ansar, captured city after city across the Nile valley. The movement is historically significant as one of the first successful anti colonial revolutions of the modern era.
para2: The uprising's climax stunned the world: after a long siege, Mahdist forces stormed Khartoum on January 26, 1885, killing the famous British general Charles Gordon, sent to evacuate the garrison, and shocking the British public. Gordon was no ordinary victim: celebrated as Chinese Gordon for commanding the Ever Victorious Army against the Taiping Rebellion, he had governed Sudan's Equatoria province in the 1870s, mapping the Nile as far south as Uganda, and his death turned avenging him into a national cause in Britain. The Mahdi himself died of illness months later, but his successor, the Khalifa Abdallahi, consolidated a stern theocratic state ruled from Omdurman, with its great mosque and fortified walls.
para3: For over a decade the Mahdist state governed most of Sudan: it minted its own coins, fielded armies of tens of thousands, fought neighbors from Ethiopia to the Congo frontier, and held off Egyptian and European attempts at reconquest. Its rule was severe, and years of war and famine bled the country.
para4: The end came with industrial war: in 1898 an Anglo Egyptian army under Kitchener, armed with machine guns and gunboats, annihilated the Mahdist host at the battle of Omdurman, and the Khalifa was hunted down and killed in 1899. Sudan passed under Anglo Egyptian rule, but the Mahdi's revolt remained a founding legend of Sudanese nationalism.

title: The Mfecane
titleline: The Mfecane - The History Web
para1: The Mfecane, the crushing, was a period of widespread warfare and forced migration that tore through southern Africa in the second and third decades of the 19th century. It was set in motion by the rise of the Zulu military kingdom under Shaka, amid drought, social unrest, and intensifying competition for the trade of Delagoa Bay, and it matters because it redrew the human map of half a subcontinent.
para2: As Zulu power expanded, tribe was set against tribe over an ever widening radius: communities were shattered, conquered peoples absorbed into new armies, and refugees fled to mountain fastnesses or across the Drakensberg, leaving devastated grasslands behind them. The disruption eased the way for white expansion into Natal and the Highveld, as Boer trekkers found lands emptied by warShaka's revolution was military as much as political: he replaced the long throwing spear with the short stabbing assegai, drilled warriors into age regiments, and perfected the encircling horns formation that made Zulu armies nearly unstoppable. .
para3: Yet the Mfecane was also an age of state building: Among the displaced were the Mfengu, shattered peoples who fled west to beg protection from the Xhosa, arriving as landless clients in a land still whole. Yet out of the turmoil rose some of the most formidable African kingdoms ever to resist colonization, the Sotho of Moshoeshoe, the Swazi, the Ndebele of Mzilikazi, and the Gaza kingdom of Mozambique. Peoples fleeing the wars carried their languages and institutions as far as Tanzania and Malawi, and the Kololo reached Zambia.
para4: The Mfecane reshaped the region's demographics and politics for good: new nations, new borders, and new capitals replaced the old order, and the memory of the crushing, its suffering and its kingdoms, still shapes identity across southern Africa today.

title: The Oyo Empire
titleline: The Oyo Empire - The History Web
para1: The Oyo Empire was a Yoruba state in what is now southwestern Nigeria that flourished from the 17th to the 19th century, though its royal traditions reached much further back, to the god king Oranmiyan, son of the founder of Ife. It matters because its horsemen built the largest empire the Yoruba people ever knew, and because its fate is bound up with the Atlantic slave trade it helped to feed.
para2: The empire's capital, Old Oyo, stood on the savanna near the Niger, where the Oyo cavalry, feared across the region, could sweep the open grasslands that forest kingdoms denied to horses. From there the Oyo subdued thirteen rival kingdoms, made vassals of neighbors like Owu and Ede, and defeated the rising kingdom of Dahomey in the wars of 1726 to 1730, collecting tribute in cloth, kola nuts, pepper, ivory, gold, and slaves.
para3: The Oyo became the central organizers of the slave trade on what Europeans called the Slave Coast, moving captives from the deep interior down to the waiting ships, and in return receiving horses, guns, and luxuries that further armed the empire. Government balanced the king, the alaafin, against a council of nobles, the Oyo Mesi, in a constitution of checks that could compel even a king to abdicate his throne.
para4: Oyo declined as civil wars between the alaafin and his nobles tore the state, the Fulani jihad pressed down from the north, and new powers like Ibadan rose from the wreckage. The empire collapsed in the early 19th century and Old Oyo was abandoned, but its culture endured, in Yoruba identity at home and, through the ships, in the diaspora of the Americas.

title: The Saadi Sultanate
titleline: The Saadi Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Saadi Sultanate ruled Morocco from 1549 to 1659, a dynasty of sharifs, claimed descendants of the Prophet, who rose in the south as champions against Portuguese intrusion and the faltering Wattasid kings. They matter because they made Morocco a power of the first rank for one brilliant generation, resisted both Portuguese crusaders and Ottoman sultans, and left Marrakesh monuments that still draw the world.
para2: The sharifs took Marrakesh, then Fez itself, uniting Morocco under their green banners and checking the Portuguese along the coast. Their finest hour came in 1578 at the Battle of the Three Kings, where the Saadi army destroyed a Portuguese invasion of Morocco and the young king Sebastian of Portugal died in the rout, a catastrophe that ended Portugal's African ambitions and reshaped Europe. Their capital still wears their splendor: the Saadian Tombs of Marrakesh rank among the city's wonders.
para3: The dynasty's most famous ruler, Ahmad al-Mansur, the Golden, ruled from 1578 to 1603 and filled his treasury with ransoms and his court with splendor: he built the ruined palace of El Badi in Marrakesh, whose vast courtyard still amazes. In 1591 he sent an army of musket men across the Sahara itself, which captured Timbuktu and broke the Songhai Empire, seizing the desert gold trade for Morocco.
para4: After al-Mansur's death the dynasty tore itself apart in civil wars between rival princes, and Morocco slid into half a century of division. Order returned only when another line of sharifs, the Alaouites, took power in 1666, but the Saadis had already fixed the mold: a Morocco united under sharifian rule, independent of the Ottomans, and reaching south across the desert sands.

title: The Scramble for Africa
titleline: The Scramble for Africa - The History Web
para1: The Scramble for Africa was the rapid, aggressive invasion, occupation, and annexation of the African continent by European powers between 1881 and 1914. In 1870 Europeans held barely a tenth of Africa, mostly coastal enclaves; by 1914 they held virtually all of it. It matters because almost everything about modern Africa, its borders, its economies, its conflicts, bears the fingerprints of those thirty years.
para2: The scramble was formalized at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, where European nations, with not one African present, wrote the rules for claiming territory and drew international borders with a cartographer's ruler, ignoring indigenous ethnic, linguistic, and political realities. The motives mixed greed and grandeur: ivory, gold, rubber, and palm oil, control of trade routes, imperial prestige, and the self appointed mission to spread Christianity and what Europeans called civilization. New tools made the interior reachable: quinine tamed the fevers that had kept Europeans on the coast, steamboats opened the Congo, Zambezi, and Niger rivers, and the long search for the source of the Nile ended at Lake Victoria in the 1860s, while diamonds at Kimberley in 1867 and gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 sharpened every appetite.
para3: The great predators were Britain and France, joined by Germany, Belgium, Portugal, and Italy. King Leopold II of Belgium took the Congo as his personal estate, where forced rubber labor killed millions, a horror that eventually shamed even his fellow imperialists. Resistance was fierce everywhere, from the Zulu and the Mahdists to the Asante and the Herero, but machine guns decided most outcomes.
para4: By the early 20th century only two African states remained free of European control: Ethiopia, which won its freedom at Adwa, and Liberia. The scramble's arbitrary borders crammed rival peoples into single colonies and split single peoples across them, and its extractive economies left colonies built to export wealth rather than grow it, a legacy the continent still confronts.

title: The Sokoto Caliphate
titleline: The Sokoto Caliphate - The History Web
para1: The Sokoto Caliphate was a massive Sunni Islamic empire founded in 1804 across what is now northern Nigeria and southern Niger, born of a jihad led by the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio. A teacher in the Hausa state of Gobir, Usman denounced the Hausa kings for mixing Islam with older practices, and his call for reform rallied both the oppressed Hausa peasants and his own Fulani people. Within seven years the old Hausa kings were gone, replaced by Fulani emirs who acknowledged the caliph at Sokoto.
para2: The result was one of the largest and most populous states in 19th century Africa: a federation of emirates, each ruled by an emir appointed in the caliph's name, bound together by Islamic law, shared scholarship, and loyalty to Sokoto. Usman's son Muhammad Bello, the second caliph, built the city of Sokoto itself and gave the empire its administrative shape, while his sister Nana Asma'u became a celebrated poet and educator of women.
para3: The caliphate is historically significant because it led a major religious and educational transformation: Islam spread deeper than ever before among ordinary people, Arabic literacy flourished, and Usman's own writings, hundreds of works in Arabic and in Fulfulde, remained the spiritual constitution of the state. The old Hausa cities, Kano, Zaria, Katsina, lived on as emirate capitals and grew richer than before.
para4: The caliphate outlasted its founders by a century, weathering wars with Bornu and internal rivalries, until British forces took Sokoto in 1903 and folded the emirates into colonial Nigeria. Yet the structure never died: the Sultan of Sokoto remains the spiritual leader of Nigeria's Muslims today, and the emirs still hold their courts.

title: The Sultanate of Zanzibar
titleline: The Sultanate of Zanzibar - The History Web
para1: The Sultanate of Zanzibar was an influential maritime empire established in 1832, when Sultan Said bin Sultan of Oman permanently moved his royal capital from Muscat to the island of Zanzibar off the East African coast. It matters because this small island became the beating commercial heart of the western Indian Ocean, the gateway through which the wealth, and the misery, of East Africa flowed to the world.
para2: Controlling a wide commercial empire along the Swahili Coast, the sultanate grew fabulously wealthy by dominating global trade in cloves, ivory, and enslaved people: Zanzibar's plantations made it the world's greatest clove producer, while its great slave market stood, notoriously, on what is now the site of an Anglican cathedral. The trade swelled on the demand for plantation labor in the Americas, which from the late 18th century made the island the pivot of the slave and ivory routes deep into Africa. Caravans financed in Stone Town pushed a thousand miles into the interior, spreading Swahili language and Islam with them.
para3: In 1861 Zanzibar was separated from Oman as an independent sultanate, but its golden age coincided with the European scramble for Africa: under Sultan Barghash, Britain and Germany divided nearly all its mainland domains between them. In 1890 Britain proclaimed a protectorate over the island itself, curtailing the slave trade and reducing the sultans to clients.
para4: The sultanate's most famous moment came in 1896, when Khalid ibn Barghash seized the throne without British approval and refused an ultimatum to step down: the Royal Navy bombarded his palace, and the Anglo Zanzibar War was over in under an hour, the shortest war in recorded history. The protectorate lasted until 1963, and a revolution soon after joined Zanzibar to Tanganyika to form Tanzania, though Stone Town, a World Heritage site, still breathes its sultanate past.

title: The Union of South Africa
titleline: The Union of South Africa - The History Web
para1: The Union of South Africa was formed in 1910 by uniting four colonies, the Cape, Natal, the Transvaal, and the Orange Free State, into a single self governing dominion within the British Empire. Born of a peace that reconciled Briton and Boer, it did so by shutting everyone else out: only whites enjoyed full political rights, and the Black majority, the vast majority, was written out of citizenship in its own land.
para2: The new state moved fast to entrench racial rule: the Natives Land Act of 1913 confined Black South Africans to a small fraction of the land, passes policed their movement, and the mines and farms ran on their cheap, controlled labor. Afrikaner nationalism, humiliated in war, triumphed at the ballot box, and in 1948 the National Party formalized the system as apartheid. Apartheid was a machine of laws: the Population Registration Act of 1950 sorted every South African by race, the Group Areas Act of 1950 tore nonwhite communities from neighborhoods now marked for whites, and in 1970 the homelands policy stripped Black South Africans of their citizenship altogether, assigning each to a Bantustan many had never seen. Together with the earlier Land Acts, the end result was more than 80 percent of the country set aside for the white minority.
para3: South Africa left the Commonwealth in 1961 and became a republic, defying mounting world condemnation. The struggle against apartheid, from the Defiance Campaign to Sharpeville, Soweto, and the townships of the 1980s, made the country a global cause, and its prisoners, above all Nelson Mandela, into symbols.
para4: Apartheid ended in 1994 with the first election open to all races, which made Mandela president. The union formed in 1910 endures as the Republic of South Africa, still wrestling with the inequalities its founders built into the ground itself.

title: The Zulu Kingdom
titleline: The Zulu Kingdom - The History Web
para1: The Zulu Kingdom was a dominant military state that emerged in Southern Africa in the early 19th century under King Shaka Zulu, who ruled from 1816 to 1828. Born the exiled son of a minor Nguni clan chief, Shaka rose in the army of the Mthethwa, then returned to claim his father's throne and forge the small Zulu clan into the terror and admiration of a subcontinent. The kingdom matters because its rise reshaped the demography of half of southern Africa and its soldiers wrote one of the most famous chapters of resistance to European conquest.
para2: Shaka revolutionized African warfare: he replaced the throwing spear with the short stabbing spear, the iklwa, paired with a large ox hide shield for close combat, and perfected the buffalo horns formation, the isiCwe, in which veteran chest and encircling horns enveloped and destroyed the enemy. Society itself was militarized, organized into age regiments, and royal expeditions marched yearly to seize cattle and tribute.
para3: The shock waves traveled far: peoples fleeing Zulu power scattered north across the Drakensberg in the great upheaval called the Mfecane, the crushing, seeding new kingdoms as far as Zimbabwe, where Shaka's rival Mzilikazi founded the Matabele state, and beyond. After Shaka's assassination by his brother Dingane in 1828, the kingdom faced the Boers and then the British, its kings ruling from the royal kraal at Ulundi.
para4: The end came in the Anglo Zulu War of 1879: King Cetshwayo's warriors annihilated a British column at Isandlwana, the worst defeat ever inflicted on a modern army by an African force, and held the line at Rorke's Drift the same night, but British reinforcements took Ulundi and divided the kingdom. Zululand was absorbed into South Africa in 1910, yet the Zulu remain South Africa's largest nation, and Shaka's name still commands the imagination of the world.

title: The Kingdom of Loango
titleline: The Kingdom of Loango - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Loango. The kingdom of Loango (c. 1550-1883) was a major state of the west-central African coast, ruling the shoreline north of the Congo River in what is now the Republic of Congo, Cabinda, and Gabon. The kingdom belonged to the Vili people, and its origins are tied to the broader Kongo world: tradition held that the founder of Loango was a kinsman of the first king of Kongo. By the sixteenth century the Loango king, the maloango, ruled from his capital at Buali and controlled a string of ports, including Loango Bay, that became famous in Atlantic trade.
para2: Loango grew rich as a commercial power. Its merchants traded ivory, redwood, copper, palm cloth, and enslaved people with the Portuguese, Dutch, French, and English traders who visited the coast, and the kingdom's brokers carefully guarded their position between the European ships and the markets of the interior. The Vili were renowned as traders and craftspeople, and Loango cloth and ivory work circulated far beyond the kingdom. Unlike Kongo to the south, Loango's rulers long kept Christianity at arm's length and preserved their own royal and religious institutions.
para3: The kingdom's political order was unusual. The maloango was a sacred ruler whose authority was balanced by powerful titled officials, and after the death of a king the throne passed among the great lineages in an elaborate system of rotation and election. In the late eighteenth and nineteenth centuries the Atlantic trade changed and then was suppressed, and Loango's ports, once centers of the slave trade, declined with it, though trade in ivory and other goods continued.
para4: The kingdom ended with the colonial partition of Africa. In the 1880s France established its authority over the coast, and by 1883 the last independent maloango had been reduced to a figurehead. Yet the kingdom's legacy endured: the Vili kept their language and traditions, and the memory of Loango, whose kings once dealt with European powers as equals, remains central to the history of the Congo coast.

title: The Kingdom of Kuba
titleline: The Kingdom of Kuba - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Kuba. The kingdom of Kuba (c. 1600-1900), lying between the Kasai, Sankuru, and Lulua rivers in what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, was one of the most sophisticated states of the African savanna. Kuba tradition remembers the kingdom's foundation by a culture hero and conqueror named Shyaam aMbul aNgoong, a hunter's son of foreign origin, who is said to have united the chiefdoms of the region in the early seventeenth century, abolished the death penalty among his people, and introduced new crops, technologies, and arts.
para2: Kuba became famous for its political organization and its art. The king, the nyim, ruled from a capital whose great court compounds were the stage for elaborate ceremony, advised by titled councils that balanced royal, aristocratic, and commoner interests. The kingdom was a federation of some twenty chiefdoms whose tribute supported the court, and its army defended the realm without the slave-raiding militarism of some neighbors. Kuba artists produced some of Africa's most admired work: raffia cloth embroidered in intricate geometric patterns, carved cups and boxes, royal portrait figures, and the celebrated ndop statues that represented individual kings.
para3: The kingdom's wealth rested on farming, fishing, and trade. Kuba markets exchanged raffia cloth, ivory, camwood, and other goods across the Congo basin, and the court grew rich controlling these routes. In the nineteenth century the Kuba resisted the slave traders who were ravaging the regions to their north and east, and the kingdom kept its independence and institutions largely intact even as chaos spread around it.
para4: Kuba's isolation ended with colonial conquest. Agents of the Congo Free State reached the kingdom in the 1880s, and after years of resistance and the turmoil of the rubber regime, Kuba was brought under Belgian colonial rule in the early twentieth century. The royal line and the court at Mushenge survived under the colonial system, and Kuba art, especially its textiles and royal statues, remains among the most treasured in the world's museums.

title: The Luba Empire
titleline: The Luba Empire - The History Web
para1: The Luba Empire. The Luba empire (c. 1585-1889) dominated the savanna woodlands of what is now the southeastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its model of sacred kingship shaped political life across a vast region. Luba tradition traces the state to a hero named Nkongolo, a cruel red-skinned king, who was overthrown by the hunter Mbidi Kiluwe from the east; their story, told in epic cycles, explained the origin of Luba kingship, in which power was legitimized by sacred blood and royal spirits called bopwe.
para2: Around 1585 the Luba king Kongolo's successors, and then the great conqueror Kalala Ilunga, expanded the state from its heartland near the Lualaba and Lomami rivers. At its height the empire stretched hundreds of kilometers, held together by a court of titleholders, provincial governors drawn from the royal clan, and a system of tribute in salt, iron, copper, ivory, and labor. Luba prestige was so great that the founders of neighboring states, including the Lunda empire to the south, claimed kinship with the Luba royal line.
para3: The empire faced new pressures in the nineteenth century. Swahili-Arab traders from the East African coast pushed deep into the interior seeking ivory and slaves, and Luba provincial chiefs gained power at the center's expense. From the 1860s the state fragmented as rival princes fought for the throne and outside raiders armed with guns destabilized the countryside. By 1889 the last effective Luba king had lost control, and the empire dissolved into warring chiefdoms that fell to Swahili warlords and then to the Congo Free State.
para4: The Luba empire left a deep mark on Central Africa. Its language became a lingua franca of the region, its royal titles and symbols were borrowed far beyond its borders, and its art, especially its sculpted stools, bow stands, and female figures embodying royal spirit mediums, is counted among the masterpieces of African art. The very idea of sacred kingship in the southern savanna carried the Luba imprint for centuries.

title: The Funj Sultanate
titleline: The Funj Sultanate - The History Web
para1: The Funj Sultanate. The Funj sultanate (1504-1821), often called the Kingdom of Sennar after its capital, ruled the Gezira and the Blue Nile valley for three centuries and brought Islam and a distinctive courtly civilization to the heart of the Sudan. The dynasty was founded by Amara Dunqas, whose people, the Funj, had risen to power in the south, and in 1504 he established his capital at Sennar on the Blue Nile, overthrowing the old Christian kingdom of Alodia in alliance with the Arab Abdallabi tribes.
para2: Under the Funj sultans, Sennar grew into a great African and Islamic capital. The sultan ruled through a court of titled nobles and governed a realm that at its height stretched from the Ethiopian borderlands to the Third Cataract, controlling tributary kingdoms such as the Taqali in the Nuba Mountains. Caravans carried gold, ivory, and slaves north to Egypt, while Islamic scholars made Sennar a center of learning whose judges and holy men shaped Sudanese religious life. The great mosques and palaces of the capital impressed every traveler who saw them.
para3: The sultanate's strength faded in the eighteenth century. The kings became prisoners of their own court: a series of palace coups brought the Hamaj regents, relatives of the queens, to real power, and the later sultans reigned as figureheads while civil wars tore the country. In 1821 the Egyptian army of Khedive Muhammad Ali, under his son Ismail Kamil Pasha, marched up the Nile, and the last Funj sultan surrendered his kingdom without a serious fight.
para4: The Funj sultanate left a lasting imprint on Sudanese identity. It spread Islam and the Arabic language through the riverain Sudan, created a political tradition that later Sudanese states claimed to inherit, and bound the lands between the two Niles into a single kingdom for three centuries. Sennar itself dwindled to a modest town, but the memory of its golden age, when its kings ruled from the mountains of Ethiopia to the cataracts of the Nile, endures in Sudanese chronicles and tradition.

title: The Emirate of Harar
titleline: The Emirate of Harar - The History Web
para1: The Emirate of Harar. The Emirate of Harar (1647-1887) was a Muslim city-state of eastern Ethiopia, centered on the ancient walled city of Harar, long regarded as a holy city of Islam in the Horn of Africa. Harar had been a center of Islamic learning and trade since the Middle Ages and the capital of the sixteenth-century conqueror Ahmad ibn Ibrahim, whose wars shook the Ethiopian highlands. In 1647 the emir Ali ibn Da'ud founded a new dynasty that ruled the city and its hinterland for two and a half centuries.
para2: The emirate was a commercial power. Harar stood at the meeting point of trade routes from the Ethiopian highlands, the Somali interior, and the Red Sea ports of Zeila and Berbera, and its merchants dealt in coffee, hides, ivory, and slaves. The walled city, with its hundreds of mosques and shrines, its markets, and its distinctive townhouses, was the economic and religious capital of the region, and Harari, the city's own Semitic language, bound its people into a close urban community. Outside the walls the emirs contended and bargained with the Oromo peoples who surrounded them.
para3: The nineteenth century brought new pressures. Egyptian forces occupied Harar in 1875 as the khedive's empire pushed into the Horn, governing it for a decade and destroying the independence of the emirate. When the Egyptians withdrew, the young Ethiopian emperor Menelik II moved in: his army defeated the last emir, Abdullahi, at the Battle of Chelenqo in 1887, and Harar was incorporated into the expanding Ethiopian Empire, with the emperor's cousin Ras Makonnen, father of the future emperor Haile Selassie, as its governor.
para4: Harar's emirate is gone, but the city endures. Its old walls, the Jugal, enclose a labyrinth of lanes that UNESCO has named a World Heritage site, and Harar remains a living center of Islamic scholarship and Ethiopian identity. The emirate is remembered as the last flowering of a tradition of Muslim city-states that for a thousand years linked the Ethiopian highlands to the wider Islamic world.

title: French West Africa
titleline: French West Africa - The History Web
para1: French West Africa. French West Africa (1895-1958) was the vast federation of French colonies that covered most of the western bulge of the continent, an area of nearly five million square kilometers. Created in 1895 and completed by conquest in the following years, it grouped eight territories: Mauritania, Senegal, French Sudan (now Mali), Guinea, Ivory Coast, Upper Volta (now Burkina Faso), Niger, and Dahomey (now Benin). The federation was ruled from Dakar by a governor-general who answered to the colonial ministry in Paris.
para2: Colonial rule was built on extraction. The French demanded taxes payable in cash, which forced farmers into wage labor and cash-crop production: peanuts in Senegal, cocoa and coffee in Ivory Coast, cotton in the Sudan. Forced labor built railways, roads, and the new port of Dakar, and African soldiers, the tirailleurs senegalais, fought for France in both world wars. A small educated elite in the Four Communes of Senegal held French citizenship, but the vast majority of Africans were subjects without rights, governed under the arbitrary indigenat code.
para3: After the Second World War the system changed. Reforms in 1946 abolished forced labor and granted citizenship, and African political parties, led by figures such as Felix Houphouet-Boigny and Leopold Sedar Senghor, pressed for self-government within a reformed French Community. In 1958 the territories of French West Africa voted in a referendum on General de Gaulle's constitution; all except Guinea chose to remain in the Community, and Guinea became independent at once. Two years later, in 1960, the remaining colonies became independent republics.
para4: French West Africa left a deep legacy. Its borders became the boundaries of eight modern states, its language, legal systems, and infrastructure still shape the region, and the memory of colonial exploitation and of the long struggle against it remains central to West African political life.

title: The Congo Free State and the Belgian Congo
titleline: The Congo Free State and the Belgian Congo - The History Web
para1: The Congo Free State and the Belgian Congo. The Congo Free State (1885-1908) was the personal colony of King Leopold II of Belgium, a territory seventy-six times the size of Belgium itself, and the site of one of the worst atrocities of the colonial age. Leopold acquired the Congo basin through diplomacy and treaties with local chiefs, and at the Berlin Conference of 1884-85 the powers recognized it as his private property. He ruled it not as a Belgian colony but as a personal estate, run for profit.
para2: Under Leopold the Congo's people were subjected to a regime of forced labor, above all in the collection of wild rubber. Companies and state agents compelled villages to meet rubber quotas through hostage-taking, flogging with the chicotte whip, and punitive expeditions that burned settlements and killed resisters. Disease, famine, flight, and violence devastated the population; historians estimate that millions died in the Congo in these decades. Missionaries and campaigners such as E. D. Morel and Roger Casement exposed the horror, and international outrage forced Leopold in 1908 to hand the Congo to the Belgian state.
para3: The Belgian Congo (1908-1960) ended the rubber terror but kept the colony under firm paternalist rule. Belgian companies mined the Katanga copperbelt and grew rich on Congolese minerals, while the administration, the church, and business ruled in alliance. Africans were denied political rights almost until the end, and when Belgium finally conceded independence in June 1960, the country had only a handful of African university graduates to run it.
para4: The consequences were immediate and tragic. Within days the Congo slid into crisis: army mutiny, the secession of mineral-rich Katanga, the murder of Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, and years of war and dictatorship followed. The Belgian period left the Democratic Republic of the Congo with railways and mines but also with a legacy of exploitation and broken institutions whose effects are still felt today.

title: German South-West Africa
titleline: German South-West Africa - The History Web
para1: German South-West Africa. German South-West Africa (1884-1915), today Namibia, was Germany's first and most important settler colony in Africa, and the scene of the first genocide of the twentieth century. The colony began in 1884 when a Bremen merchant, Adolf Luderitz, acquired land on the coast and Berlin declared a protectorate. German settlers and companies pushed inland, seizing the cattle and the best grazing land of the Herero and Nama peoples, whose herds were the basis of their wealth.
para2: Rising dispossession provoked war. In 1904 the Herero rose under Chief Samuel Maharero, and after initial victories the Germans counterattacked with overwhelming force under General Lothar von Trotha, who issued an extermination order and drove the Herero into the Omaheke desert to die of thirst. The Nama under Hendrik Witbooi then rose in a guerrilla war that lasted until 1908. Between 1904 and 1908 roughly three-quarters of the Herero and half of the Nama people perished; survivors were confined in concentration camps such as Shark Island or forced into labor.
para3: After the wars the colony was rebuilt as a settler state. Diamonds were discovered near Luderitz in 1908, railways linked the interior to the coast, and German immigration grew, with Africans confined to reserves and bound by harsh pass and labor laws. The German period ended in the First World War, when South African forces invaded in 1915 and Germany surrendered the territory.
para4: South-West Africa then passed to South Africa under a League of Nations mandate, beginning seventy-five years of South African rule and apartheid. Namibia finally became independent in 1990. The memory of the genocide remained alive among the Herero and Nama, and in 2021 Germany formally recognized it as genocide and pledged reparations, more than a century after the events.

title: Portuguese Angola and Mozambique
titleline: Portuguese Angola and Mozambique - The History Web
para1: Portuguese Angola and Mozambique. The Portuguese colonies of Angola and Mozambique were the oldest and among the last European possessions in Africa. Portugal's presence dated to the late fifteenth century, when its ships reached the Kongo coast and the Swahili ports, and by 1575 Paulo Dias de Novais had founded Luanda, the base from which Portugal slowly pushed into the Angolan interior. In Mozambique, Portuguese rule spread from coastal towns such as Mozambique Island and Sofala up the Zambezi valley, where settlers held vast prazo estates.
para2: For centuries the colonies rested on the slave trade. Angola became the largest single source of enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic, above all to Brazil, and the trade devastated the peoples of the interior while enriching merchants and the coastal towns. When the Atlantic slave trade was finally suppressed in the nineteenth century, Portugal turned to territorial conquest: after the Berlin Conference it fought a series of campaigns to occupy the interior, crushing the kingdoms and peoples of Angola and Mozambique by the early twentieth century.
para3: Twentieth-century rule was built on forced labor and settler privilege. African farmers were compelled to grow cotton and to work on plantations and roads, while Portugal encouraged white immigration and kept education for Africans minimal. After 1961 liberation movements rose in both colonies: the MPLA, FNLA, and UNITA in Angola, and FRELIMO in Mozambique. Portugal fought long counterinsurgency wars that drained its army until the Carnation Revolution of 1974 in Lisbon ended the dictatorship, and both colonies became independent in 1975.
para4: Independence was followed by devastating civil wars, fueled by the Cold War and by regional powers, which lasted in Angola until 2002 and in Mozambique until 1992. The Portuguese colonial period left the two countries with a shared language, cities such as Luanda and Maputo, and a bitter legacy of exploitation and war that shaped their modern history.

title: Italian Libya
titleline: Italian Libya - The History Web
para1: Italian Libya. Italian Libya (1911-1943) was born of invasion. In 1911 Italy, hungry for empire, declared war on the Ottoman Empire and landed troops in Tripoli, claiming the Ottoman provinces of Tripolitania and Cyrenaica. The conquest was far harder than Rome expected: Libyan resistance, led above all by the Sanusi religious order and later by the guerrilla leader Omar Mukhtar, tied down Italian armies for two decades, and Italy's effective control long extended little beyond the coast.
para2: Under Fascism the conquest turned brutal. Mussolini's regime resolved to pacify Libya completely, and from 1923 Italian forces reconquered the interior region by region. In Cyrenaica the war against Omar Mukhtar's guerrillas was waged with aerial bombing, poison gas, and the deportation of the Bedouin population into concentration camps, where tens of thousands died of hunger and disease. Mukhtar was captured and hanged in 1931, and with his death organized resistance collapsed. The human cost of the pacification was catastrophic: a large share of Cyrenaica's people perished or was displaced.
para3: In 1934 Italy united Tripolitania, Cyrenaica, and the Fezzan into the colony of Libya, and in 1939 declared it part of metropolitan Italy, the so-called Fourth Shore. The regime poured money into roads, ports, and farms and settled tens of thousands of Italian colonists on confiscated land, especially in the fertile Gebel and along the coast, intending Libya as a permanent Italian province.
para4: The colony died in the Second World War. Libya became a major battlefield, and by 1943 British forces had driven the Italians and Germans out. After the war the United Nations decided Libya's fate, and in 1951 the country became independent under King Idris. The Italian period left Libya transformed: its cities reshaped, a settler community that soon departed, and a population scarred by a conquest remembered as a national tragedy.

title: The Lunda Empire
titleline: The Lunda Empire - The History Web
para1: The Lunda Empire. The Lunda empire (c. 1660-1887) arose among the Lunda people of the upper Kasai and Lulua rivers, in what is now the southern Democratic Republic of the Congo, and grew into one of the largest states of the southern African savanna. Lunda tradition ties its kingship to the Luba hero Mbidi Kiluwe, whose son is said to have married the Lunda queen Lueji, uniting the two royal lines. From this union came the title of Mwata Yamvo, borne by the Lunda emperors, whose court at Musumba became the ritual and political heart of a vast realm.
para2: The Mwata Yamvo's authority radiated outward through a remarkable system of government. Royal relatives and titled officials governed the provinces, while outlying chiefs ruled as vassals, sending tribute in ivory, slaves, copper, salt, and cloth to the capital and receiving royal emblems in return. Lunda prestige was magnetic: adventurers and princes carried the Lunda model of kingship far abroad, founding related dynasties among the Kazembe on the Luapula, in what is now Zambia, and deep into modern Angola.
para3: The empire's power in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries rested heavily on trade. Lunda brokers dominated the routes carrying ivory and enslaved people both westward to the Portuguese in Angola and eastward toward the Swahili traders of the East African coast, and the Mwata Yamvo grew rich on the traffic. But the trade also destabilized the state: armed rivals, ambitious provincial chiefs, and new trading powers eroded the center, and by the later nineteenth century the empire was breaking apart.
para4: The end came with colonial conquest. In the 1880s the lands of the Mwata Yamvo were partitioned between Leopold's Congo Free State and British and Portuguese claims, and in 1887 the last great Mwata Yamvo died as his empire disintegrated. Yet the Lunda political legacy survived in the chieftaincies it had planted across the savanna, and the Mwata Kazembe of the Luapula valley, heir to a branch of the Lunda royal line, remains a living traditional ruler today.

title: The Rif War
titleline: The Rif War - The History Web
para1: The Rif War. The Rif War (1921-1926) was the great Berber uprising against Spanish colonial rule in northern Morocco, and one of the most remarkable anti-colonial struggles of the twentieth century. Spain had held a protectorate in northern Morocco since 1912, but its authority barely reached beyond the coastal towns into the mountains of the Rif. In 1921 a Spanish column under General Silvestre pushed deep into the Rifian highlands, where it was met at the hill of Annual by Rifian fighters led by the judge and scholar Abd el-Krim.
para2: The Battle of Annual was a catastrophe for Spain: the Spanish army was annihilated, losing some ten thousand men, and huge stores of rifles, machine guns, and artillery fell into Rifian hands. Abd el-Krim followed the victory by proclaiming the Rif Republic, with its capital at Ajdir, and set about building a state with ministries, an army, and diplomatic contacts abroad. For five years the republic controlled most of the Rif, and Abd el-Krim became an international symbol of resistance to empire.
para3: Spain alone could not recover. In 1925 Abd el-Krim struck into the French zone of Morocco, threatening Fez itself, and France joined the war. The two colonial powers combined their forces, landed a great army at Alhucemas Bay, and crushed the republic between converging columns, using aircraft and, on the Spanish side, chemical weapons against the Rifian tribes. Outnumbered and starved, Abd el-Krim surrendered in May 1926 and was exiled to Reunion.
para4: The Rif War left a deep mark. It shook the Spanish state and helped bring on the dictatorship of Primo de Rivera, it taught colonial armies lessons in modern counterinsurgency, and it made Abd el-Krim a hero of Moroccan nationalism and of anti-colonial movements everywhere. The Rif Republic, though short-lived, is remembered as one of the earliest attempts to build a modern independent state in defiance of European empire.

title: The Italo-Ethiopian Wars
titleline: The Italo-Ethiopian Wars - The History Web
para1: The Italo-Ethiopian Wars. The Italo-Ethiopian Wars (1895-1937) decided whether Africa's oldest independent state would survive the age of empire. Italy, newly united and eager for colonies, had seized Eritrea on the Red Sea and in 1889 signed the Treaty of Wuchale with the Ethiopian emperor Menelik II. The Italian text of the treaty made Ethiopia an Italian protectorate; the Amharic text did not. When Menelik repudiated the Italian version, war followed.
para2: The First Italo-Ethiopian War ended in a stunning African victory. In 1895-96 Italian columns advanced from Eritrea into the highlands, and on 1 March 1896 Menelik's great army, some one hundred thousand strong, destroyed the invaders at the Battle of Adwa. It was the most decisive defeat of a European power by an African state in the whole colonial era. Italy recognized Ethiopian independence, and Adwa became a beacon of pride for Africans and people of African descent across the world.
para3: Forty years later Mussolini sought revenge and empire. In October 1935 Italian armies invaded Ethiopia from Eritrea and Somalia in the Second Italo-Ethiopian War. This time the invaders brought aircraft, tanks, and poison gas, used against soldiers and civilians alike, while the League of Nations failed to stop them. Emperor Haile Selassie's armies were overwhelmed, Addis Ababa fell in May 1936, and Italy proclaimed its East African empire, though Ethiopian patriots fought on in the mountains.
para4: Italian rule lasted only five years. In 1941 British and Commonwealth forces, alongside Ethiopian resistance fighters, liberated the country and restored Haile Selassie. Ethiopia emerged as a founding member of the United Nations, its independence vindicated twice over. Adwa remains a national holiday and a symbol of African resistance, while the memory of the occupation and its atrocities still shapes Ethiopia's view of its past.

title: The Algerian War
titleline: The Algerian War - The History Web
para1: The Algerian War. The Algerian War (1954-1962) was the bitter struggle that ended 132 years of French rule in Algeria and became one of the defining conflicts of the age of decolonization. Algeria was no ordinary colony: a million European settlers, the colons or pieds-noirs, held its best land, and France declared Algeria to be France itself. Algerian Muslims, denied equal rights, had risen before, and the massacre of thousands at Setif in 1945, after victory in Europe, convinced many that only force would win freedom.
para2: On 1 November 1954 the National Liberation Front, the FLN, launched its uprising with coordinated attacks across the country. The war that followed was fought in the mountains and the cities alike. The FLN's army, the ALN, waged guerrilla war from the djebel, while in Algiers the Battle of the Casbah in 1956-57 brought bombings, mass arrests, and systematic torture by French paratroopers into the world's headlines. France poured half a million soldiers into Algeria and resettled two million villagers into camps, yet could not destroy the rebellion.
para3: The war shook France to its foundations. In 1958 the colons and the army, fearing abandonment, rose in Algiers and brought down the Fourth Republic, returning Charles de Gaulle to power. De Gaulle slowly concluded that Algeria must go; when diehard generals tried to stop him with a putsch in 1961 and the secret OAS waged a campaign of terror, he pressed on. In March 1962 the Evian Accords ended the war, and Algeria became independent on 5 July 1962.
para4: The cost was immense: hundreds of thousands of Algerians dead, and a million colons who fled to France, along with many Algerian harkis abandoned to brutal reprisals. In Algeria the FLN built a one-party state on the memory of liberation, and the war's legacy still shapes Algerian identity and Franco-Algerian relations today.

title: The Mau Mau Uprising
titleline: The Mau Mau Uprising - The History Web
para1: The Mau Mau Uprising. The Mau Mau Uprising (1952-1960) was the great revolt of the Kikuyu people of Kenya against British colonial rule, and one of the decisive blows against empire in Africa. Its roots lay in land: white settlers had taken the fertile Kenya highlands, while the Kikuyu, the largest people of the colony, were crowded into reserves or worked as squatters on settler farms. After the Second World War, returning African veterans and the growing city of Nairobi turned land hunger into militancy.
para2: From the late 1940s a secret movement bound its members by oaths to fight for land and freedom, and in October 1952 the colonial government declared a state of emergency. The rebels, calling themselves the Kenya Land and Freedom Army but known to the world as Mau Mau, took to the forests of the Aberdare mountains and Mount Kenya, where fighters such as Dedan Kimathi and Stanley Mathenge led a guerrilla war against the British, while supporters in the reserves and in Nairobi passed food, guns, and information.
para3: The British response was overwhelming and brutal. Tens of thousands of Kikuyu were detained in camps where beatings, forced labor, and torture were routine; more than a million villagers were forcibly resettled into fortified villages. By 1956 the army had broken the forest fighters, and Dedan Kimathi was captured and hanged in 1957. Perhaps eleven thousand rebels died, against some two hundred colonial soldiers and police, though the detention system claimed many more lives.
para4: The emergency could not save the colony. The revolt convinced Britain that Kenya must move to African rule, and in 1963 Kenya became independent under Jomo Kenyatta, himself jailed for years as the alleged Mau Mau leader. The rising transformed Kenya's politics, and its veterans are honored today as heroes of independence, while Britain has since paid compensation to surviving victims of its camps.

title: The Apartheid State
titleline: The Apartheid State - The History Web
para1: The Apartheid State. Apartheid, meaning separateness in Afrikaans, was the system of racial rule imposed on South Africa after the National Party won the all-white election of 1948. Racial segregation was nothing new in South Africa, but the Nationalists made it total. Laws classified every person by race, forbade marriage and intimacy across the color line, reserved jobs by race, and separated schools, hospitals, transport, and whole neighborhoods. At its heart lay the land: Africans, the overwhelming majority, were confined to thirteen percent of the country.
para2: The system was enforced with relentless machinery. Every African had to carry a pass, and hundreds of thousands were arrested each year for being without one. The 1950s saw the Group Areas Act uproot whole communities, Bantu Education degrade black schooling, and the creation of the bantustans, ethnic homelands meant to strip Africans of South African citizenship altogether. The African National Congress answered with the Defiance Campaign and the Freedom Charter of 1955, and after police killed sixty-nine peaceful protesters at Sharpeville in 1960, the ANC and the Pan Africanist Congress were banned and their leaders, Nelson Mandela among them, turned to underground struggle and eventually imprisonment on Robben Island.
para3: Resistance and repression deepened together. The 1976 Soweto uprising of schoolchildren against Afrikaans schooling was met with gunfire and inspired a new generation; strikes, boycotts, and township revolts in the 1980s made the country increasingly ungovernable, while worldwide sanctions and isolation squeezed the economy. The white state fought back with emergency rule, death squads, and wars against its neighbors, but it could not win.
para4: In 1990 President F. W. de Klerk unbanned the ANC and freed Mandela, and after years of negotiation South Africans of all races voted in April 1994 in the election that made Mandela president. Apartheid left South Africa with deep wounds of inequality, but its defeat, by the people it oppressed, remains one of the great moral victories of the twentieth century.
