title: The Kingdom of Rwanda
titleline: The Kingdom of Rwanda - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Rwanda. The kingdom of Rwanda (c. 1600-1961) was one of the most centralized and enduring states of the African Great Lakes region. According to tradition, the kingdom was founded by Gihanga, the ancestor of the Nyiginya royal line, and over the centuries the Tutsi kings, the mwami, extended their rule over the hills of modern Rwanda. By the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, under warrior kings such as Yuhi IV Gahindiro and Kigeli IV Rwabugiri, Rwanda had grown into a powerful military state dominating its neighbors.
para2: Rwandan society was organized around kingship, cattle, and clientship. The mwami was a sacred ruler, guarded by elaborate court ritual, and below him the people were ordered into lineages of Tutsi, Hutu, and Twa, bound together by the cattle clientship called ubuhake, in which a patron granted cattle in return for service. Armies of warriors, drawn from lineages across the kingdom, raided for cattle and defended the realm, while royal capitals moved among the hill courts, the most famous being Nyanza, with its great thatched royal palace.
para3: European rule transformed and hardened the old order. Germany claimed Rwanda in the 1890s, and after the First World War Belgium ruled it together with Burundi as Ruanda-Urundi. The colonizers governed through the mwami and the Tutsi chiefs, and their rule, and later their favoritism toward one group and then the other, sharpened the divisions of Rwandan society. In 1959, as independence approached, a Hutu revolution overthrew the monarchy amid massacres of Tutsi, and the kingdom was abolished in 1961.
para4: The legacy of the kingdom still shapes Rwanda. The social divisions codified under the monarchy and the colonial state fed the tragedies that followed, culminating in the genocide of 1994. Yet the old kingdom also left Rwanda its language, its unity as a nation, and symbols of statehood, from the royal drums to the palace at Nyanza, that Rwandans still claim as their heritage.

title: The Kingdom of Burundi
titleline: The Kingdom of Burundi - The History Web
para1: The Kingdom of Burundi. The kingdom of Burundi (c. 1680-1966) was, with Rwanda, one of the two great monarchies of the African Great Lakes region. Tradition traces its foundation to a king named Ntare, founder of the dynasty whose kings, the mwami, bore a cycle of four names: Ntare, Mwezi, Mutaga, and Mwambutsa. Over two centuries the kingdom grew from a small hill state in the east of the country to rule most of modern Burundi, expanding under kings such as Ntare Rushatsi and Mwezi Gisabo.
para2: Burundi's monarchy rested on a distinctive balance of power. The mwami was a sacred figure, associated with the fertility of the land and guarded by ritual, but real power was contested among the royal princes, the ganwa, who governed the provinces and often fought one another and the king for control. Below them, chiefs and sub-chiefs collected tribute from a farming people of Hutu, Tutsi, and Twa, bound to their lords by clientship and by the sacred royal drums, especially the great drum Karyenda, the emblem of the kingdom.
para3: Colonial rule came late and ruled lightly through the throne. Germany took Burundi in the 1890s, and after the First World War Belgium governed it as part of Ruanda-Urundi, working through the mwami and the ganwa. Unlike in Rwanda, the monarchy survived into independence: Burundi became independent in 1962 as a kingdom under Mwambutsa IV. But rivalry between the palace and the politicians, and growing Hutu-Tutsi violence, brought coups and counter-coups, and in 1966 the young Ntare V was overthrown and the monarchy abolished by Michel Micombero.
para4: The kingdom's end opened decades of military rule and ethnic bloodshed. Yet Burundi's monarchy left the country a strong sense of its own nationhood, and the royal drummers of Burundi, heirs of the court tradition, still perform today as a living symbol of the kingdom and its culture.

title: Italian Somaliland
titleline: Italian Somaliland - The History Web
para1: Italian Somaliland. Italian Somaliland (1889-1960) was Italy's colony on the Horn of Africa, created piece by piece along the Benadir coast. Italy had acquired the port of Aden and footholds on the coast in the 1880s, and in 1889, as the European powers partitioned the Somali lands, it established protectorates over the southern sultanates and founded Mogadishu as its capital. For years Italian rule barely reached beyond the coast, and the interior was controlled by the Sayyid Muhammad Abdullah Hassan, whose dervish movement fought the Italians, British, and Ethiopians for two decades until 1920.
para2: Under Fascism the colony was tightened and used as a springboard. In 1935-36 Italian Somaliland served as the southern base for the invasion of Ethiopia, after which it was folded into the vast Italian East Africa. Roads were built, plantations of bananas and cotton spread along the Shabelle and Juba rivers, worked by coerced Somali labor, and Mogadishu was rebuilt as a colonial capital. The empire collapsed quickly: in 1941 British forces conquered Italian East Africa, and Somaliland passed under British military administration.
para3: After the war Italy returned under a United Nations trusteeship. From 1950 the Italian administration, working with the Somali Youth League and other parties, prepared the territory for self-government, establishing schools, elections, and a Somali administration. The trusteeship ended on schedule, and on 1 July 1960 Italian Somaliland became independent, uniting five days later with the former British Somaliland to form the Somali Republic.
para4: The colonial period left Somalia with its capital at Mogadishu, an educated elite, and the infrastructure of the south, but also with the legacies of plantation labor, regional imbalance between north and south, and the boundaries that still define the troubled politics of the Horn.

title: British Somaliland
titleline: British Somaliland - The History Web
para1: British Somaliland. British Somaliland (1884-1960) was the British protectorate on the southern shore of the Gulf of Aden, created to supply the port of Aden with meat. In 1884-86 Britain signed treaties of protection with the Somali clans of the north coast, establishing a territory centered on the port of Berbera. British rule was deliberately light: the protectorate was governed cheaply, through the clans and their elders, and for years the interior was left largely to itself.
para2: The protectorate's quiet was shattered by the long war against Muhammad Abdullah Hassan, the leader the British called the Mad Mullah. From 1899 his dervish movement, based in the interior, fought the British, Italians, and Ethiopians in a twenty-year struggle that became legend in Somali memory. Four British expeditions failed to catch him until 1920, when the new Royal Air Force bombed his strongholds from the air, one of the first campaigns of its kind, and the movement collapsed; the Sayyid died later that year.
para3: After 1920 the protectorate settled into modest development: Berbera's trade, a small administration, schools, and a Somali police force. In the Second World War Italy briefly occupied the territory in 1940 before British forces retook it in 1941. After the war, nationalist feeling grew with the Somali Youth League, and Britain prepared the protectorate for independence. On 26 June 1960 British Somaliland became independent, and five days later it united with the former Italian Somaliland as the Somali Republic.
para4: The protectorate's story did not end there. When Somalia collapsed in 1991, the north revived its old colonial identity and declared itself the Republic of Somaliland, restoring the independence of 1960. Though unrecognized internationally, Somaliland has governed itself since, making the legacy of the British protectorate a live question in the Horn of Africa to this day.

title: The Republic of Liberia
titleline: The Republic of Liberia - The History Web
para1: The Republic of Liberia. The Republic of Liberia (1847-present) is Africa's oldest modern republic, founded by free Black people from the United States. From 1820 the American Colonization Society, supported by slaveholders and abolitionists alike, settled freed African Americans on the Grain Coast of West Africa, where they founded Monrovia, named for President Monroe. The settlers, known as Americo-Liberians, established towns along the coast, and in 1847, pressed by Britain and France to assert sovereignty, the colony declared independence under its first president, Joseph Jenkins Roberts.
para2: The young republic faced a difficult existence. Its people, never more than a small minority, ruled a coast of trading towns while the African peoples of the interior, including the Kru, Grebo, and Vai, resisted settler control for generations. Britain and France nibbled at its borders, and the government survived on customs revenue, foreign loans, and the flag of convenience it sold to foreign shipping. Only in the early twentieth century, with armed frontier forces, did Monrovia extend real control over the hinterland, imposing on its peoples taxes and forced labor that drew international scandal.
para3: Modern Liberia was shaped above all by William V. S. Tubman, president from 1944 to 1971, who opened the country to foreign investment, especially the Firestone rubber plantations and iron ore mining, and extended citizenship to the interior peoples. Yet power and wealth remained concentrated in Monrovia and among the settler-descended elite of the True Whig Party. In 1980 soldiers led by Samuel Doe overthrew and killed President William Tolbert, ending 133 years of Americo-Liberian rule.
para4: What followed was tragedy: a decade of dictatorship and then two devastating civil wars between 1989 and 2003 that killed a quarter of a million people. Since the peace, Liberia has rebuilt under elected governments, including Ellen Johnson Sirleaf, Africa's first elected female president. The republic's history, born of freedom in America and forged through rule, resistance, and war, remains unique on the continent.

title: The Congo Crisis
titleline: The Congo Crisis - The History Web
para1: The Congo Crisis. The Congo Crisis (1960-1965) was the chaotic struggle that followed the independence of the Belgian Congo, and it became one of the first great battlegrounds of the Cold War in Africa. Belgium had ruled the Congo for half a century without preparing it for self-government, and when independence came on 30 June 1960, under President Joseph Kasa-Vubu and Prime Minister Patrice Lumumba, the new state had almost no trained administrators, officers, or engineers.
para2: The country disintegrated within days. The army mutinied against its Belgian officers, Belgium sent in troops, and on 11 July the mineral-rich province of Katanga declared independence under Moise Tshombe, backed by Belgian mining interests. Lumumba appealed to the United Nations, which sent a peacekeeping force, but when it refused to crush the Katanga secession, he turned to the Soviet Union. In September the army chief Joseph Mobutu seized power, and Lumumba was arrested, flown to Katanga, and murdered there in January 1961, with the complicity of Belgian officials and the knowledge of Western intelligence services.
para3: For four more years the Congo was torn by rival governments, secession, and rebellion. UN forces finally ended the Katanga secession in 1963, but in 1964 a great revolt, the Simba rebellion, swept the east and took Stanleyville before Belgian and American-backed mercenaries crushed it. In 1965 Mobutu seized power for the second time, beginning the thirty-two-year dictatorship that renamed the country Zaire.
para4: The crisis scarred the Congo and the continent. It cost perhaps a hundred thousand lives, destroyed the country's most charismatic leader, entrenched foreign interference in Congolese politics, and turned the Cold War's deadliest African conflict into a warning of what could follow independence. The murder of Lumumba remains a symbol of the promise of decolonization betrayed.

title: The Egyptian Revolution of 1952
titleline: The Egyptian Revolution of 1952 - The History Web
para1: The Egyptian Revolution of 1952. The Egyptian Revolution of 1952 overthrew the monarchy that had ruled Egypt for a century and a half and set the country on the path of Arab nationalism. The old order had been discredited by corruption, by the continued presence of British troops in the Suez Canal Zone, and above all by the humiliating defeat of the Egyptian army in Palestine in 1948. Within the army a secret group of young officers, the Free Officers, organized by Gamal Abdel Nasser, blamed the king and his politicians for the disaster and plotted to seize power.
para2: In the early hours of 23 July 1952 the Free Officers struck, taking over army headquarters and the key points of Cairo without a fight. General Muhammad Naguib, a respected senior officer, was placed at their head. King Farouk abdicated three days later and sailed into exile on his yacht, and in June 1953 the monarchy was abolished and Egypt declared a republic. The new regime at once launched a sweeping land reform, breaking up the great estates that had dominated Egyptian rural life.
para3: Nasser soon outmaneuvered Naguib and in 1954 took power himself, becoming the most influential Arab leader of the century. His government forced the British out of the Canal Zone, nationalized the Suez Canal in 1956 and survived the tripartite invasion that followed, built the Aswan High Dam, and championed Arab unity and non-alignment, carrying Egypt's influence across the Arab world and beyond.
para4: The revolution transformed Egypt and the Middle East. It ended the rule of the old landowning elite, expanded education and industry, and inspired military coups and nationalist movements across the Arab world, though it also entrenched the army in power. The republic born in July 1952 still governs Egypt, and Nasser's image remains a touchstone of Egyptian and Arab politics.

title: The Suez Crisis
titleline: The Suez Crisis - The History Web
para1: The Suez Crisis. The Suez Crisis of 1956 was the showdown that broke the old colonial order in the Middle East. On 26 July 1956, President Gamal Abdel Nasser of Egypt nationalized the Suez Canal Company, the Anglo-French enterprise that ran the waterway linking the Mediterranean to the Red Sea. The move, prompted by the American and British refusal to finance the Aswan High Dam, electrified the Arab world and enraged London and Paris, which saw Nasser as a threat to their empires and their oil routes.
para2: Britain and France resolved to retake the canal by force, in secret collusion with Israel. On 29 October 1956 Israeli forces invaded the Sinai; Britain and France, posing as peacemakers, then issued an ultimatum they knew Egypt would reject, bombed Egyptian airfields, and landed troops at Port Said. Militarily the operation succeeded, but politically it was a catastrophe: the world was outraged, the United Nations condemned the invasion, and the United States and the Soviet Union, in rare agreement, demanded withdrawal.
para3: Under crushing American financial and diplomatic pressure, the British and French pulled out within weeks, and Israel withdrew from Sinai the following spring. A United Nations emergency force was stationed on the Egyptian border, the first peacekeeping mission of its kind. Nasser, defeated in the field, emerged as the political victor and the hero of Arab nationalism.
para4: The crisis marked the end of Britain and France as independent great powers in the Middle East; the humiliation helped topple Prime Minister Anthony Eden. It confirmed American dominance in the region's affairs, emboldened Arab nationalism and non-alignment, and left the canal firmly in Egyptian hands. The next round of the Arab-Israeli conflict, in 1967, would close the canal again, but 1956 had already changed the rules of the game.

title: The Merina Kingdom of Madagascar
titleline: The Merina Kingdom of Madagascar - The History Web
para1: High in the cool central highlands of Madagascar, the Merina people built the kingdom that would eventually unite almost the entire island under one crown. Emerging around 1540 under King Andriamanelo, the Merina realm began as one of many small chiefdoms scattered across the Imerina plateau, where rice terraces climbed the hillsides and fortified hilltop towns crowned the ridges. The kingdom spent much of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries divided among rival branches of the royal family, but that fragmentation ended when a gifted ruler named Andrianampoinimerina conquered the competing kingdoms one by one and reunited Imerina by about 1794.
para2: Andrianampoinimerina organized his realm with remarkable care. He regulated rice cultivation, organized markets at set locations, codified laws, and famously declared that the sea would be the boundary of his rice field, announcing his ambition to rule the whole island. His son Radama I, who reigned from 1810 to 1828, made enormous progress toward that goal. With British military instructors, modern firearms, and an alliance with the British governor of Mauritius, Radama conquered the eastern port of Toamasina and then much of the island. Antananarivo, the capital, grew into a city of tens of thousands, and European missionaries arrived to set up schools and introduce a Latin alphabet for the Malagasy language.
para3: The most famous Merina ruler was Queen Ranavalona I, who reigned from 1828 to 1861 and pursued a dramatic reversal of her husband's pro-European policies. Determined to protect Merina sovereignty and traditions, she expelled missionaries, banned Christianity among her subjects, and cut back foreign contacts while still expanding her armies and building industries with the help of the French artisan Jean Laborde. Her reign preserved Malagasy independence for a generation, though at the cost of international isolation and harsh internal campaigns that devastated parts of the island. Later monarchs, including Radama II, Rasoherina, and Ranavalona II, reopened the kingdom to outside influence and made Protestant Christianity the court religion.
para4: The Merina kingdom's independence ended in the 1890s as French imperial ambitions in the Indian Ocean turned toward Madagascar. France invaded in 1883 and again in 1895, capturing Antananarivo in September of that year. Queen Ranavalona III was forced to accept a French protectorate, and in 1897 she was exiled to Algeria while the monarchy was abolished. The royal palace complex, the Rova of Antananarivo, still crowns the highest hill of the capital as a symbol of the kingdom. Today Madagascar's population is heavily descended from Merina and other Malagasy peoples, and the Merina dialect remains the basis of the national language.

title: The Gold Coast under British Rule
titleline: The Gold Coast under British Rule - The History Web
para1: The Gold Coast was Britain's most important West African colony and the first sub-Saharan African colony to win independence, becoming the nation of Ghana in 1957. European contact with this coast began in 1471 when Portuguese sailors landed and found so much gold being traded that they named it the Gold Coast. The Portuguese built Elmina Castle in 1482, the first European fort in sub-Saharan Africa, and over the following centuries the Dutch, Danes, Swedes, and British all built fortified trading posts along the shore. By the eighteenth century the British had become the dominant European power, and their forts at Cape Coast and elsewhere served the trade in gold, ivory, and tragically, enslaved people.
para2: British rule over the Gold Coast developed gradually. In 1821 the British government took over the coastal settlements from a merchant company, and after the Anglo-Ashanti wars of the nineteenth century, the coastal region was formally declared the Gold Coast Colony in 1874. The powerful Asante kingdom in the interior resisted British expansion for decades, fighting a series of wars that culminated in the War of the Golden Stool in 1900, led by the queen mother Yaa Asantewaa. By 1902 the Asante kingdom and the Northern Territories had been incorporated, giving the colony roughly its modern boundaries.
para3: Under colonial rule the Gold Coast's economy was transformed by cocoa. Introduced in the late nineteenth century, cocoa farming spread rapidly among African farmers, and by the 1920s the Gold Coast was the world's largest cocoa producer. The colony developed railways, harbors, and schools, and an educated African elite emerged in coastal towns like Accra and Cape Coast. This elite founded early nationalist organizations, including the Aborigines' Rights Protection Society in 1897 and the United Gold Coast Convention in 1947. After the Second World War, demands for self-government grew stronger, fueled by returning veterans and economic hardship.
para4: The push for independence was led by Kwame Nkrumah, who returned to the Gold Coast in 1947 and founded the Convention People's Party in 1949 with the slogan of self-government now. Through strikes, boycotts, and electoral victories, Nkrumah's movement forced Britain to concede a series of constitutional reforms. Nkrumah became prime minister in 1952, and on March 6, 1957, the Gold Coast became independent Ghana, with Nkrumah declaring that the independence of Ghana was meaningless unless linked to the total liberation of Africa. Ghana's independence inspired decolonization movements across the continent.

title: The Dervish State
titleline: The Dervish State - The History Web
para1: The Dervish State was an Islamic resistance movement and proto-state that fought British, Italian, and Ethiopian forces in the Horn of Africa for two decades, making it one of the longest anti-colonial struggles in African history. It was founded in 1899 by Mohammed Abdullah Hassan, a Somali religious scholar and poet whom the British nicknamed the Mad Mullah, a label that badly underestimated his abilities. Hassan had studied in Mecca and belonged to the Salihiyya Sufi brotherhood, and he returned to Somaliland preaching religious renewal and resistance to Christian colonial encroachment.
para2: The movement drew its strength from the Somali clans of the interior, especially the Dhulbahante and Warsangali, who supplied thousands of mounted spearmen. The Dervishes built a network of stone forts across the arid interior, with their capital eventually established at Taleh, where impressive fortifications still stand. Hassan proved a master of guerrilla warfare, and his forces defeated or eluded four separate British military expeditions between 1901 and 1904. The British suffered a humiliating disaster at Dul Madoba in 1913, when a Dervish force annihilated a colonial constabulary unit, killing its commander, Richard Corfield.
para3: The Dervish struggle was sustained partly by Hassan's extraordinary poetry, which served as propaganda, news, and rallying cry in a society with a rich oral tradition. His poems mocked his enemies, celebrated victories, and called the faithful to resistance, and they were memorized and recited across Somali-speaking lands. The movement also received some support from the Ottoman Empire and later from the German-allied Lij Iyasu of Ethiopia during the First World War, when the Dervishes were recognized as allies and Hassan was styled emir.
para4: The Dervish State finally fell to the technological superiority of the post-war British military. In January and February 1920, the Royal Air Force carried out the first major aerial bombing campaign in Africa, attacking the forts at Taleh and the Dervish concentrations. The ground offensive that followed, combining British, Somaliland, and King's African Rifles troops, overran the strongholds in a matter of weeks. Hassan fled to Ethiopia, where he died of illness in December 1920. The Dervish resistance became a founding legend of Somali nationalism, and Hassan is remembered today as a national hero in Somalia.

title: German Kamerun and Togoland
titleline: German Kamerun and Togoland - The History Web
para1: Kamerun was Germany's largest African colony on the continent's west coast, established during the Scramble for Africa and lost during the First World War. In July 1884, the German explorer Gustav Nachtigal arrived off the Cameroon coast and signed treaties with the Duala chiefs at the settlement then called Kamerunstadt, planting the German flag just ahead of British and French rivals who also coveted the region. The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885 confirmed German possession, and over the following decades the colony expanded far into the interior, eventually covering an area larger than Germany itself.
para2: The German colonial administration ruled Kamerun from the coastal capital of Buea, at the foot of the towering volcanic Mount Cameroon. The colony's economy was built on plantations, and German companies established vast estates growing rubber, cocoa, palm oil, and bananas in the fertile coastal lowlands. Plantation agriculture depended on forced and poorly paid African labor, and conditions were often brutal. Resistance flared repeatedly: the Duala and other coastal peoples protested land seizures and taxes, while uprisings in the interior, including those of the Bafut and other highland peoples, were suppressed by German-led punitive expeditions.
para3: Despite its harshness, German rule brought infrastructure and development to parts of the colony. Railways were built from the port of Douala into the interior, and a second line linked Yaoundé, the new inland capital, toward the highlands. Mission schools and medical stations spread, and German scientists conducted research in the colony's forests, which were among the most biologically rich in Africa. By 1914 Kamerun had a population of several million Africans and a few thousand German settlers, administrators, and soldiers.
para4: The First World War ended German rule in Kamerun. In August 1914 British and French forces invaded from Nigeria and French Equatorial Africa, beginning the Kamerun campaign. The German Schutztruppe, outnumbered and cut off from resupply, conducted a fighting retreat into the mountainous interior and held out until February 1916, when the remaining garrison crossed into neutral Spanish Guinea and was interned. After the war the colony was divided between Britain and France as League of Nations mandates, with France taking the larger eastern share. These mandates became the independent nations of Cameroon and parts of Nigeria in 1960 and 1961.

title: Spanish Morocco and Equatorial Guinea
titleline: Spanish Morocco and Equatorial Guinea - The History Web
para1: Spain's African empire was a modest remnant of a once-global dominion, consisting of territories in Morocco, Western Sahara, and Equatorial Guinea. Spain's presence in North Africa stretched back to the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries, when it seized the coastal enclaves of Ceuta and Melilla, but the modern colonial empire dated from the late nineteenth century. In 1884-1885 Spain claimed the stretch of coast that became Spanish Sahara, and in 1912, by agreement with France, it received a protectorate over the northern zone of Morocco, a mountainous region inhabited mainly by Berber peoples.
para2: Governing the Moroccan protectorate proved costly and violent. Spain never fully controlled the Rif mountains, and in 1921 a Spanish army was annihilated at the Battle of Annual by Rifian forces under Abd el-Krim, losing around ten thousand men in one of the worst colonial defeats of the century. Abd el-Krim proclaimed the Republic of the Rif, and it took a combined Franco-Spanish campaign of over three hundred thousand troops, in which the young Francisco Franco made his reputation, to crush the resistance by 1926. The experience forged the Spanish Army of Africa, whose officers would launch the military rising of 1936 that began the Spanish Civil War, when Franco airlifted his troops from Morocco to the mainland.
para3: Spanish Guinea, in central Africa, consisted of the island of Fernando Po and the mainland territory of Río Muni. Spain had acquired Fernando Po in 1778 but only developed it in the twentieth century, turning the island into a profitable cocoa colony worked by migrant laborers recruited under conditions widely condemned as near-slavery. Río Muni, home mainly to the Fang people, remained thinly administered until after the Second World War. In 1959 Spain reorganized its Guinean territories as provinces of Spain itself, a response to growing international pressure for decolonization.
para4: Decolonization came rapidly in the late twentieth century. Spain withdrew from the Moroccan protectorate in 1956 when Morocco gained independence, though it kept Ceuta, Melilla, and the small enclave of Ifni until 1969. Equatorial Guinea became independent in 1968, and its first president, Francisco Macías Nguema, established one of Africa's most brutal dictatorships. In 1975, as Franco lay dying, Spain abandoned Western Sahara, which was promptly partitioned between Morocco and Mauritania, triggering a conflict over the territory that remains unresolved today.
